title: Short Stuff: Dingoes!
summary: Short Stuff episode on dingoes. Josh and Chuck open with banter about their Australia trips and a dingo encounter at a game ranch, then discuss whether dingoes are dogs or their own species (Canis familiaris vs. a separate species, possible relation to Southeast Asian and East Asian dogs), their coat colors by habitat, breeding and pup-rearing (about five or six pups a year, weaning around two months, staying with parents for about a year), and maturity by six to seven months. They cover dingoes as a pest to livestock, the roughly 5,000 km dog fence built in the nineteenth century, dingoes as apex predators that keep kangaroo populations in check, and hybridization with domestic dogs (about a third of southeastern Australian dingoes are hybrids). They note dingoes rarely bark and mostly howl. The episode closes with the Lindy Chamberlain case: the 1980 disappearance of baby Azaria at a campsite, her murder conviction based largely on circumstantial evidence including the missing matinee jacket, the 1986 discovery of the jacket after a climber's death, her release, and the later coroner's inquest that cleared her and amended the death certificate (the hosts cite 2012). The episode ends with a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and game ranch dingo encounter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about the episode and recall their Australia trips, including a dingo experience at a game ranch where they walked into a dingo pen. Chuck says he didn't see dingoes on his trip.

segments.title: Dingo vs. dog: species classification
segments.summary: They discuss whether dingoes are dogs, noting they are descended from the same line as domestic dogs. They mention Canis familiaris and a later claim that dingoes are a separate species, and a study linking dingoes to Southeast Asian and East Asian dogs such as the Shiba Inu.

segments.title: Dingo appearance and habitat
segments.summary: Dingo coat color varies by habitat: ginger with white feet near the usual shape, golden yellow in deserts, darker brown or nearly black near forest edges. Water is the main limit on where they live, since they are opportunistic feeders.

segments.title: Dingo breeding, pups, and maturity
segments.summary: Dingoes breed once a year and have five or six pups, raised in sheltered spots such as rock areas, wombat burrows, rabbit warrens, or hollow logs. Pups wean at about two months, and may leave or stay around a year. They are fully equipped to be on their own by six to seven months.

segments.title: Dingoes as livestock pests, the dog fence, and apex predation
segments.summary: Dingoes are considered a pest by the livestock industry, which built a fence about 5,000 kilometers long in the nineteenth century to protect sheep grazing land. As apex predators they hunt kangaroos and keep populations in check, and there is a debate about letting them back past the fence. Hybridization is also discussed, with about a third of southeastern Australia's dingoes thought to be hybrids with domestic dogs.

segments.title: Dingo barking and howling
segments.summary: Dingoes supposedly don't bark, and communicate by howling and by other sounds. Chuck says they can bark but tend not to.

segments.title: Lindy Chamberlain case and the dingo baby story
segments.summary: The hosts recount the Azaria Chamberlain disappearance at a campsite in Australia, the murder conviction of her mother Lindy Chamberlain (played by Meryl Streep in Cry in the Dark), and the role of the missing matinee jacket in the conviction. The jacket was found in 1986 after a climber's death, and Lindy was released. A later inquest cleared her and amended the death certificate.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh talk about trying to pet the dingoes, which did not want to be petted, and the episode closes with the standard Short Stuff sign-off and iHeartRadio credit.
